item.title: More money for this war? This rigmarole won't wash
item.description:
The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission.

You shouldn’t go to war without the backing of the U.S. Congress. President Donald Trump is learning that the hard way, as his — not our — six-month-and-counting “little excursion” and “small potatoes” Iranian quagmire drags on. And you don’t build weapons for tomorrow’s wars — especially the ones you say are critical to future victories (remember them?) — using the parliamentary peek-a-boo prestidigitation known as reconciliation. In both instances, Trump is seeking big changes in U.S. national security as unilaterally as possible, with minimal congressional backing.

Reconciliation is a controversial process to fund programs. It doesn’t have to follow the standard congressional appropriation rules. Most critically, reconciliation bills aren’t subject to a Senate filibuster. That means they can pass the so-called upper house with a simple majority vote, instead of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster. Predictably, that too often leads to rickety resourcing and reversed reckonings when the other political party takes over.

“Unfortunately, reconciliation is becoming a hallmark of the slow but steady degradation of Congress,” Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, Director of Advocacy here at the Project On Government Oversight, says. “It has also become a tantalizing tool for the Pentagon in its never-ending quest to throw good money after bad, to the tune of hundreds of billions above and beyond what a complicit Congress already showers them with each year.”

And while you can begin a war with a surprise attack, you can’t build weapons that way. Yet Trump is trying to employ this reconciliation rigmarole in his proposed 2027 defense budget for arguably his two top military priorities — his “Golden Dome” aerial shield, and his wholesale push to develop sky-darkening fleets of drones:

— The Pentagon is seeking $17.9 billion for Golden Dome next year, but only $400 million (2.2%) is in its official budget request.

— The Pentagon’s drone-centric Defense Autonomous Working Group (DAWG) is asking for $54.6 billion in 2027, but only $1 billion (1.8%) is in the Defense Department’s official base budget request.

While it looks like Congress will eventually approve Trump’s bloatacious $1.1 trillion defense budget, the separate $350 billion reconciliation proposal appears to be going down in flames (the combined $1.45 trillion top line represents an incredible 44% boost over this year’s budget). Yet it’s that threat to the $350 billion that’s got the generals in charge of those two programs sounding the alarm. “If they don’t figure it out, there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding,” Space Force General Michael Guetlein, chief of the space-shield effort, said flatly last month.

Army Lieutenant General Steven Marks (PDF) told a defense-industry confab September 9 that his DAWG drone programs will lose their “momentum” if they don’t get at least some of the $53.6 billion plus-up requested. Marks warned that potential U.S. foes “can take a $100,000 drone and conduct an attack against a $2 billion vessel,” but declined to elaborate on potential funding cuts. “Unfortunately, all of our systems are all classified,” he said, “and so I will not be talking in detail about those.”

Well, here’s a safe bet that’s not secret. The Pentagon will not get much, if any, of its $350 billion reconciliation bonus. That will force it to cut key operations and maintenance accounts, assuming it wants to keep Golden Dome and its drone programs humming. And those cuts in O&M — training, fuel, parts, and all the other humdrum items that hone a force’s fighting edge — will dull the readiness of the U.S. military.

Bottom line: U.S. national security needs to be built on solid bipartisan bedrock, and not the ever-shifting sands of fleeting political advantage.


Playing defense is becoming a bigger business


It’s kind of funny that the Department of Defense putatively changed its name to the Department of War just when it’s becoming more of a department of defense than ever. The exploding use of drones around the world has forced the U.S. military back on its heels. The offensive edge that the U.S. has arguably held since World War II is being eclipsed by swarms of flying autonomous AI-guided weapons that can cheaply elude the Pentagon’s costly defenses. All of a sudden, they have made defending what the U.S. military has just as vital as what the U.S. military attacks. Impressive U.S. military assets — aircraft carriers, bombers, armored divisions — that once ruled the seas, skies, and battlefields, are now targets. And the U.S. military is scrambling to protect them:

— After Iranian drones and missiles battered U.S. bases in the Middle East, the Air Force announced September 3 that it wants to buy “a Ground-Based, Medium-Caliber Gun Weapon System that fires affordable munitions, enables defense against air and missile threats with an initial focus on subsonic cruise missiles and Unmanned Aircraft Systems to provide persistent defense in support of United States Air Force assets.”

— The Air Force’s top general says the wide use of drones and missiles in Iran and Ukraine have convinced the service that “we have to create a new career field and have experts in the ability to defend your airfield from all of these threats.”

— Early in the Iran war — 22 days after six U.S. troops were killed by an Iranian drone — the Air Force issued a call for “prefabricated, transportable, hardened shelter systems designed to protect personnel from blast and fragmentation threats” that could be shipped to Jordan.

— Two days later, the Pentagon sought contractors to “plan and design a hardened, underground, secure, Combat Center Building and squadron operations buildings supporting a variety of airframe and missions to include, but not limited to, bombers, fighters, and unmanned aircraft systems for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance” at the key U.S. base in Qatar. Iran knocked out that command post at Al Udeid, which had run U.S. air campaigns in the region for more than two decades, in the war’s opening weeks. The Pentagon has yet to detail the damage.

— Iran also severely damaged the Navy’s key base in the Persian Gulf, home of its 5th Fleet, early in the conflict. “They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao recently said, adding that the service is “looking” at what to do with it, without elaboration. The service is “not getting back in [the base in Bahrain] anytime soon,” Admiral Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, said August 31. The Pentagon has yet to detail the damage.

— In August, the Pentagon’s Mobile Land-Based Sensors Projects Office said it is looking to develop “highly mobile, rapidly deployable” Forward-Based Mode Radar Next systems “capable of providing enhanced early warning, tracking, and discrimination of emerging missile threats” under its Nimble Options for Buying Layered Effects — NOBLE — contracting authority (thank God at least one of those terms was deemed acronym-worthy).

— The Air Force wants to convert cargo planes into “adaptive, force-multiplying launch platforms” that provide “a rapidly deployable swarm [of drones] for base security.”

— Last month, the Marines began buying counter-drone vehicles “capable of detecting, tracking, and defeating unmanned aerial threats while maintaining the flexibility to reposition as mission requirements evolve.” The $1.9 million buggies are outfitted with Hellfire missiles originally designed for the Army’s AH-64 Apache helicopter gunships.

All this is fine and dandy. We need to defend our forces. The trouble is that offense is much cheaper than defense. Given that financial advantage, the attacker can overwhelm the defender. Basically, the attacker has to succeed only once, while the defender must succeed 24/7/365. That’s why building moats, the Great Wall of China, and the Maginot Line — not to mention Golden Dome (grandchild of Safeguard, and child of the Strategic Defense Initiative) — is ultimately a losing game.

Retooling subs for a bigger, cheaper, punch


Last month, the Navy changed the designation for 19 of its future Virginia-class submarines from SSN — naval shorthand for a fast-attack submarine — to SSGN, meaning a guided-missile submarine. But the new nomenclature goes far, ahem, deeper than a single letter.

The service is stretching the original design of the 377-foot Virginia-class boats by 84 feet so the number of Tomahawk cruise missiles it can carry grows from “about 37 to about 65,” according to long-time Navy expert Ronald O’Rourke at the Congressional Research Service. The change shifts the new subs’ primary mission from attacking enemy subs to striking land targets up to 1,000 miles away from beneath the waves. The goal is to replace the firepower of the four bigger Tomahawk-carrying Ohio-class subs which are reaching the end of their service life.

The new expanded subs will cost about $4 billion each. That’s a lot of money, but it’s cheaper than designing and building a new class of submarines. And that’s refreshing, given the Pentagon’s current gimme-more mindset. The hardware tweak is a timely reminder that it is possible to do more with less. “It illustrates that innovation in the military is not always about inventing a new technology,” Joshua VerGow and Abigail Rudolph wrote recently for the Atlantic Council. The U.S. military, they add, “should make building from scratch the exception rather than the default.”

Here's what has caught The Bunker's Eye recently


The dogfight continues

Some in Congress are fighting to keep 126 Air Force A-10 Warthog attack planes flying until 2034 over the service’s objections, Military.com’s Haley Fuller reported September 7. Ground-pounders love the warplane and its gatling gun, dedicated to coming to their aid if they run into trouble on the battlefield; the Air Force has been saying for years that role can be filled by other aircraft. The lawmakers have dubbed their bill the BRRRRT Act, for Bolstering Recognition, Resurgence, Retention, and Remembrance of the Thunderbolt Act. “Thunderbolt” is the A-10s official name, but troops affectionately call it the Warthog…and “BRRRT” is the distinctively deadly sound — listen here — of its gun.

Aurora bombsoverus

The Pentagon now has weapons orbiting the Earth, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said September 14, the first public acknowledgement that the U.S. is arming the heavens, the Air Force said in a press release.

What 9/11 did to them

A trio of unlikely U.S. military veterans who signed up to fight following the terror attacks 25 years ago reflect on the “pride, regret, frustration and gratitude” their service wrought, Dave Philipps reported in the September 10 New York Times.

Speaking of gratitude, thanks for stopping by The Bunker this week. Once again, we’re taking a couple of weeks off, returning October 7. Meanwhile, consider forwarding this on to friends and foes so they can subscribe here.

item.title: A Trump-Zelensky meeting and another exercise in futility
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine met President Donald Trump for a brief 40 minutes on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly meeting in New York on Tuesday. According to reports, both looked optimistic and shared comments to that end.

“I hope we will end this war, and President Trump will help us end this war,” Zelensky said during the meeting. “I think we need to do this as quick as possible — before winter.”

According to the New York Times, “the U.S. president nodded and repeated his words with approval.”

But a closer look reveals that there was no breakthrough, just more suggestions that a face-to-face meeting between Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin might be on the horizon. Although both expressed a desire to see the war end, there is little evidence that it will.

Right now, all the big foreign policy tickets in town make Trump look like a failure. If he wants to roll into the midterms with a fighting chance of avoiding the loss of both chambers, then something has got to give.

While I believe his intentions to be sincere, he has failed to bring peace to Ukraine, despite saying he would do so within 24 hours. His war of choice in Iran has made the U.S. military look weak and left the global economy staggering towards a depression.

Moreover, the late Lindsey Graham bequeathed to him the hot potato of risking another tariff war against China and India just weeks before the midterms.

In the face of resistance from Zelensky and his European sponsors,Trump has been flailing when it comes to muscling through a peace deal for Ukraine. Indeed, in the teeth of rising diesel prices, he has begged Zelensky not to bomb Russian oil refineries. His entreaties have fallen on deaf ears. At the presser after their meeting, Zelensky suggested that the issue wasn’t discussed.

The Ukraine war is stuck in a retaliation loop in which Russia will always respond in kind to Ukraine’s attacks on its infrastructure.The only difference is that Russia has the strategic capabilities, specifically the economic weight, readily available energy, deep industrial base, and population size to continue slugging away for much longer than Ukraine.

Because of this, Ukraine’s energy infrastructure will once more get battered by massive strikes over the winter months. Hot on the heels of the September Yalta Economic Security Conference in Kyiv, Zelensky wants one thing: continued Western support – weapons and money — to keep fighting at least through to April 2026.

That is foolhardy in the extreme. Trump cannot will the U.S. defense industrial sector to produce more interceptors overnight. America has burned through 80% of its THAAD stock since the Iran war started, as well as two-thirds of its own Patriots.

While Trump touched on the idea of an energy ceasefire in his meeting with Zelensky, it is unlikely that Russia will get on board. Disrupting Muscovites’ access to gasoline is far less damaging politically than starving people in Ukrainian cities of heat and light. Why would Russia agree to give Zelensky some winter respite only for Ukraine to come out swinging again in the spring? Pause and reload has become predictable.

Moreover, Trump seems unable to extricate himself from the war against Iran. No matter the positive spin he puts on it, like in his remarks at the U.N. on Tuesday, the conflict in the Middle East is taking a new and more dangerous turn with the Houthis now occupying the east bank of the Bab al Mandeb. The U.S. Navy has a base on the opposing shore in Djibouti, but then so does China, its only foreign military outpost.

With the new sanctions bill, Trump can choose to sign a national security or he can re-impose tariffs of up to 100% on China and India, which would no more likely to succeed than in 2025. Such tariffs would, however, de facto impose an additional tax on ordinary Americans who have seen gasoline prices shoot up. This, on the basis of analysis from 2025 that up to 90% of the cost of tariffs imposed on Chinese exporters was passed on to U.S. consumers.

That leaves Trump with no good options, staring down the barrel of becoming a lame duck President in early November.

The cold truth is that Trump is deeply tied up in all of the foreign policies which have failed and he can no longer distance himself from them. For as much as he talks peace in Ukraine, the U.S. is still selling billions of dollars worth of weapons to the Ukrainians with European money to keep the fight going.

For his part, Zelensky has proven remarkably effective in shuttling around the world cajoling, brow beating, and occasionally shaming his interlocutors into providing the money and military materiel that Ukraine needs. Yet the truth is that no amount of support for Ukraine, four and a half years into this terrible war, will ever be enough.

I align myself with John Mearsheimer’s assessment that the Ukraine war will be settled by Russia on the battlefield. Zelensky seems incapable of accepting that Ukraine will eventually lose Donetsk, come what may.

For him, the end of the war likely means the end of his political career in Ukraine, at least for the foreseeable future. He is expected to lose a future Presidential election.

The next Ukrainian president in peacetime will face different, though no less formidable challenges than Zelensky has faced in wartime. Their country will be bankrupt and European sponsors may feel more coy about providing the level of financial assistance that they provide now. The demographic picture looks terrible in a country where around half of the adult population still in the country is a pensioner.

The Canadian move to explore Associate Membership of the EU in the future may offer a troubling harbinger of what may lay in store for Ukraine. Subsidy rich states like Poland and France will not be willing to share the European budget with new members, however much they suffered in war.

But these are Ukraine’s problems, not America’s. Zelensky showing up again and insisting that Ukraine really can win, with a few more weapons and a bit more money, is the last thing that Trump needs right now. The U.S. president needs a diplomatic success if he holds any hope of avoiding a shredding in the midterms. The Greenland deal won’t be enough. And Zelensky isn’t budging, perhaps because he sees that Trump may have even less leverage over him from November.

item.title: Trump and 14 Lat Am leaders ignite new drug-terror war at UN
item.description:
On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York on Tuesday, 14 Latin American and Caribbean countries followed the Trump administration’s lead by designating 24 cartels, prison gangs, and drug trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), laying the groundwork for potential U.S. military involvement in operations across the Western Hemisphere.

The announcement came from the majority of the member-states of the Shield of the Americas, a loosely-formed coalition of 19 right-leaning regional governments — including Colombia, Argentina, Chile and Peru — which in March committed to use lethal military force against criminal groups alleged of drug trafficking to the United States.

The Shield members that — for reasons not immediately clear — did not sign Tuesday’s statement include Guatemala, Jamaica, Belize and Bahamas. Other hemispheric governments led by nominally left-of-center leaders, such as Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Venezuela, Uruguay, Nicaragua, Cuba and several Caribbean nations — some of which are regional epicenters for organized crime — have not been invited to join the ad-hoc coalition.

The joint declaration, which invoked the 1947 mutual defense pact known as the Rio Treaty, came just hours after President Trump told world leaders that “the cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere.” As such he was previewing what many believe may signal the acceleration of open-ended, ill-defined, and unauthorized U.S. military deployments across wide swaths of Latin America and Caribbean in a fusion of the war on drugs with the war on terror.

“For years, the cartels have waged war against the people of this hemisphere. Now, we’re waging war on them,” Trump told several heads of state, including Ecuadorean President Daniel Noboa, Honduran President Nasry Asfura, and Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz, at the gathering of the consortium being led by ousted Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Tuesday’s announcement followed statements last month by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at a Panama gathering of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (AC3), the Shield's operational wing, that five countries — Ecuador, Colombia, Honduras, Jamaica and Guatemala — had authorized U.S. forces to conduct joint military operations against armed groups in their national territory. Since March, Ecuador has been hosting U.S. special forces in joint operations near the border with Colombia, which has agreed to host the organization’s regional headquarters in Medellín. Colombia also plans to borrow three U.S. MQ-9A reaper drones to carry-out precision strikes against high-value targets and is slated to receive $1 billion in fresh U.S. security assistance over an undefined period of time.

While Tuesday’s joint declaration also highlighted plans to boost economic cooperation and multilateral coordination, the coalition’s principal objective is “to do bad things to bad people,” Hegseth told the senior military leaders assembled in Panama, warning them of the alleged threats also posed by irregular migration and extrahemispheric actors like China.

Tuesday’s meeting came a week after U.S. officials announced that $52 million in foreign military financing would be redirected from African and European countries to Ecuador, Colombia, Peru and Panama. More recently, defense officials speaking with CNN said that “most” of the Pentagon’s high-powered drones operating in Africa will likely be transferred to South America in anticipation of escalating, land-based counternarcotics and counter-terrorism operations.

While most, if not all, of the region’s leaders understand the acute challenges to their societies posed by organized crime, experts and former officials say that coercive pressure must act in concert with law enforcement-led solutions and economic development, as well strengthening the rule of law, combatting public corruption, and disrupting illicit financial flows, if security strategies are to prove durable over time.

item.title: In Red Sea crisis, Somaliland seizes leverage for US recognition
item.description:
The president of Somaliland took advantage of the geopolitical and global economic turmoil caused by the Iran War to visit Washington this week in an effort to advocate for American recognition of Somaliland and for the deepening of economic ties between the two.

President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, made a public appearance at the Hudson Institute on September 14, where he argued that his country’s three-and-a-half decade run as a secure, self-governing actor warranted recognition from the United States. Irro also said that, although he’s “not a geologist,” experts tell him his country has “everything” the U.S. could want in terms of critical minerals, which he’d be happy to provide the U.S. in exchange for deeper relations.

A self-proclaimed sovereign country widely considered to be part of Somalia by the international community, Somaliland has for decades struggled to gain recognition on the international stage. But Israel’s unexpected decision in December 2025 to be the first government in the world to recognize Somaliland as an independent state has raised questions about which other countries might follow suit. Somaliland denies that recognition came as part of a quid-pro-quo arrangement, but, shortly after the recognition, it was reported that Somaliland will be forming a security partnership with Israel, potentially including offering the Israelis military access to its territory.

If there was ever a moment for Somaliland officials to make the case for recognition, now is indeed the time. Somaliland sits in one of the world’s most geostrategically significant locations. With roughly 530 miles of coastline along the Gulf of Aden — which connects to the Red Sea through the vitally important Bab el-Mandeb Strait — Somaliland is at the heart of a crucial shipping route and on the edge of the expansive battlefield of the Iran War.

Somaliland’s major port city of Berbera is located just across the Gulf from the Yemeni coast, putting Somaliland’s major economic engine within striking distance of potential Houthi attacks.

The Houthi rebels — an Iran-aligned militant group fighting the Yemeni government and its Saudi backers in Yemen’s devastating civil war — have played a major role in expanding the footprint of the ongoing Iran War. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted ships traversing the Red Sea as well as energy and logistics infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

Their stunning gains along Yemen’s southwest coast in recent weeks — including the capture of the major port city of Mocha, near Bab el-Mandeb — mean the Houthis are increasingly in control of the Yemeni coastline along the strait, which gives the group added leverage. Indeed, if a lasting peace deal remains elusive, Iran could aim to use the Houthis’ position to effectively shut down shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, which is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point.

This would essentially mirror the Iranian strategy on the Strait of Hormuz, which sits on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. By shutting down shipping through both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, the Iranians and their allies would essentially bring to a halt nearly all sea trade connecting the Middle East to the Indian Ocean, worsening the ongoing global supply shock, especially as it relates to energy. The greater the pain on the world’s pocketbook, the greater the likelihood, the Iranians believe, that pressure will mount to a point where the United States and Israel have no choice but to negotiate an honest end to the war.

Irro’s argument for recognition is straightforward. Somaliland has been operating as a functional and relatively secure country since claiming independence from Somalia in 1991. It has its own military and police force, and has a coast guard that patrols its waters along the Gulf of Aden, defending against potential threats from pirates and other nefarious actors on the seas. In an appeal to traditional Western appreciation for democracy, Irro argues that Somaliland’s ability to hold consistent (though often delayed) elections is another indicator of its ability to govern well.

But the Hudson Institute appearance was unsteady. Irro, aged 70, giggled seemingly uncontrollably throughout, and struggled to articulate a vision for the broader region. At one point, he compared neighboring Sudan to Venezuela, saying — like the Latin American country — Sudan is “too far away” from Somaliland for him to provide an opinion on its civil war, despite the fact that the two are only about 460 miles apart.

Cameron Hudson, a former U.S. intelligence official specializing in Africa, said on X that Irro “did himself and his country a major disservice by being unprepared or incapable of being able to respond convincingly to serious topics that will determine his country’s future. It was like watching an African Biden.”

Last Tuesday, Irro held a breakfast with a bipartisan group of members of Congress from both chambers as well as a group of ambassadors. The president also met individually with several members of Congress, including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.), Rep. John Rose (R-Tenn.) and Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), with whom he reportedly discussed a wide variety of issues pertaining to security, trade, and investment.

In addition to meeting with American officials, Irro met with members of the Israeli embassy in Washington, including the country’s ambassador.

Ever since Trump took office, Somaliland has seen an opportunity to push for American recognition. Last year, the breakaway state offered the United States the opportunity to open up a military base along its Gulf coast in exchange for recognition, which the Trump administration reportedly seriously considered. Ultimately, though, concern over how such recognition would complicate U.S. relations with nearby governments in the region ultimately dissuaded the American president from agreeing to the arrangement. Such recognition would also hurt American relations with Somalia, which remains a major counterterrorism partner in the fight against the al-Qaeda affiliate al-Shabaab.

Nevertheless, American military presence in the region appears to be growing. Recent reporting suggests the U.S. has sent military personnel to Somaliland’s eastern neighbor Puntland, another region claiming independence from Somalia.

Despite a fraying federal system and deep insecurity, Somalia is still a member of both the African Union and Arab League, allowing it to maintain close ties with its regional neighbors. U.S. recognition of Somaliland would risk hurting American relations with this broad base of countries across the Middle East and Africa.

In terms of what Somaliland is willing to provide the U.S. for recognition (or at least for enhanced relations), Irro told Semafor he would consider offering greater military access — including potentially building a military base (as he has offered before) — as well as access to the country’s deep resources. In an appeal directed right at Trump, Irro also suggested the possibility of naming the airport in the major port city of Berbera, which has one of the longest runways on the continent, after the American president.

Still, it’ll be a challenge for Somaliland’s leadership to persuade the United States to recognize it while Somalia remains an American partner in counterterrorism activity, and while the wider regional community opposes Somaliland’s independence. But if either of these factors change, and if the Gulf region remains a hotbed for conflict, global geopolitical and military positioning will, at the very least, keep the conversation going.

The United Nations was created, its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.

The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.

‘The Dragon’ defined: How three capitals reimagined China
item.description:
Few things better illustrate how charged the American debate over China has become than the reaction to Jennifer Kavanagh’s recent proposal for a radically different U.S. military posture in Asia.

Kavanagh, a senior fellow at Defense Priorities, has argued that Washington should pull most of its forces back from the “first island chain,” which includes Taiwan and the Philippines, toward the more defensible “second island chain,” while narrowing its defense commitments to regional allies and eschewing any commitment to defend Taiwan.

The proposal prompted a sharp backlash from analysts and commentators, with some flinging accusations that Kavanagh and her colleagues are “fifth columnists.”

The episode raises a larger question: how did the American debate over China become so intensely focused on strategic competition – and so resistant to arguments for restraint?

David M. McCourt’s "The Dragon Defined: How Washington, Canberra, and London Reimagined China" is an unusually illuminating account of how China came to be understood as a strategic competitor in the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom.

A professor of sociology at the University of California, Davis, McCourt draws on more than 250 interviews with diplomats, strategists, academics, and other participants in the foreign-policy communities of the three countries to provide a rich, transnational account of great help to those seeking to understand the debate surrounding the rise of China.

As McCourt puts it in the preface, “There is no single, real China, only numerous aspects – some inviting, others threatening. What leaders and elites see is largely a reflection of themselves: their hopes and fears for their countries domestically and on the world stage.” It is an apt summary of a sociologist’s perspective – and an especially useful one given the book’s subject: the production and circulation of elite knowledge.

China, in McCourt’s telling, is both an empirical object and a kind of mirror. Its actual behavior matters, but so too do the institutions, professional incentives, domestic political struggles, and national self-conceptions through which that behavior is interpreted. This helps explain the striking transformation McCourt documents. In the 1990s, Washington approached China with considerable confidence that American power and engagement could shape the direction of its rise. By the mid-2010s, that confidence had given way to what McCourt describes as “an insecure, anxious, even fearful US hegemon facing a risen China that has become a near-peer challenger.”

The shift from engagement to strategic competition was consequently not simply a response to an objective change in China. It was also a change in the way American elites understood the United States and its place in the world. ⁠

McCourt focuses on the institutions where foreign-policy knowledge is made – government agencies, think tanks, universities, journalism, and the business community – and, crucially, the individuals who inhabit them.

American readers will recognize many of the names: AEI, CSIS, government agencies, prominent China scholars, journalists, and the revolving door connecting all of them. But McCourt’s comparative approach makes the equivalent institutions in Britain and Australia equally familiar and their relationships intelligible, including Chatham House, the Lowy Institute, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, the SOAS China Institute, and the Australian Institute of International Affairs.

For an American reader, the most revealing story is what happened inside Washington. The shift away from engagement did not begin with a single administration, nor did it happen because everyone suddenly reached the same conclusion about China. For decades, American policy had rested in part on an expectation that economic development, integration into international institutions, and the growth of a Chinese middle class would produce some degree of political liberalization and convergence.

McCourt shows that this expectation was never universally shared. The U.S. military, in particular, had long maintained a more skeptical view of China. As one military analyst told McCourt, his organization had “stayed in the same place” while the rest of the China field had “recently ‘come to us.’” The rise of strategic competition was therefore not simply the triumph of a new idea; in important respects, it was the movement of one longstanding interpretation of China from the margins of the policy community toward its center.

A look at the beginning of the George W. Bush administration illustrates the point nicely. Before September 11, 2001, Bush described China as a “strategic competitor.” Of course, the terrorist attacks and the wars that followed redirected American strategic attention elsewhere for years. China did not disappear as a concern, but the question of how to manage its rise drew less attention. When great-power competition returned to the center of U.S. strategy, some of this skepticism reemerged.

The assumptions underpinning engagement became increasingly difficult to sustain. Economic growth had produced a much more powerful China, but not the political transformation many American policymakers had anticipated. President Xi Jinping’s consolidation of power, Beijing’s more assertive foreign policy, concerns about technology and economic dependence, human-rights abuses, and fears about the balance of power in East Asia all contributed to a growing sense that the old approach had failed.

McCourt is especially interested in what happened to the people whose professional identities had been built around the older paradigm. One former Engager describes the pressure bluntly: in Washington, “You’re here because you want to influence policy,” which means asking, “how do I stay credible?” The choice, as he put it, was whether to “adjust myself to the metanarrative” or become “a voice in the wilderness.” McCourt’s interviews suggest careerism was not incidental to the production of China knowledge. Scholars, analysts, journalists, and think-tank experts had to connect their work to the concerns of policymakers – and the definition of what counted as relevant policy expertise was itself changing.

At the same time, institutions with reasons to oppose engagement were becoming more influential. The military was hardly alone: hawkish think tanks and national-security officials had long challenged the assumptions of engagement, while parts of the business community became disillusioned with the expectation of an endlessly expanding “China market.” Politicians and strategists from across the political spectrum increasingly emphasized different aspects of the same emerging problem: China’s challenge to American power, its political system, its economic practices, or the security of the U.S.-led order in Asia. Figures such as Kurt Campbell, Ely Ratner, Robert Blackwill, Robert Work, Matthew Pottinger, and Elbridge Colby occupied different positions in this evolving debate, but the larger shift was institutional.

By the early 2020s, the proposition that engagement had failed had hardened into a premise of Washington discourse, even as scholars and former Engagers, such as Michael Swaine and J. Stapleton Roy, continued to dispute the historical record.

This is where McCourt’s comparative cases become particularly instructive. Australia, for example, complicates the assumption that ideas about China simply flow from Washington outward. McCourt shows how Australian analysts and officials helped strengthen arguments that subsequently gained traction among American skeptics of engagement, while initiatives such as the Indo-Pacific concept and AUKUS demonstrate that allies can also shape American strategic thinking.

The point is not that any one of these actors “caused” America to become hawkish on China. It is that the American understanding of China emerged from a field of institutions and individuals whose interests, experiences, and assumptions were changing at the same time.

McCourt’s field theory provides a useful way of understanding these developments without requiring either conspiracy or simplistic material determinism. Individuals occupying similar institutional positions, exposed to similar incentives and professional networks, can come to remarkably similar conclusions. Conversely, individuals situated differently can interpret the same Chinese actions in radically different ways.

That is perhaps the greatest contribution of "The Dragon Defined." It does not require the reader to accept any particular interpretation of China in order to appreciate the importance of understanding how interpretations of China are made.

For anyone interested in the origins of the contemporary turn from engagement toward strategic competition, McCourt has produced an exceptionally rich account. Its many individual case studies and interviews resist easy summary, and the comparative perspective makes the book considerably more illuminating than a study focused exclusively on Washington.

Whatever position one takes on China, American grand strategy, or the wisdom of strategic competition, "The Dragon Defined" offers an important reminder: before asking what China is, it is worth asking who is doing the defining – and why.

Navigating a More Uncertain World: Lessons from CIA’s Red Cell
item.description:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States is confronting yet another era of profound uncertainty and potential dangers. The pace and scale of change are creating unforeseen disruptions that impact our security, stability, and prosperity. Advancing technologies are being adopted and applied in unexpected ways, sparking debates about the unintended consequences for human existence. No longer can we sit back and wait to be surprised.

In the wake of 911, the CIA stood up the Red Cell to address a systemic failure of imagination and later reaffirmed this mission after the intelligence failures of the Iraq War. As memories have faded, the appetite for bold, contrarian thinking has waned, but we remain one unforeseen act of violence, one slow-burning and overlooked development, one scientific breakthrough away from the next shock. In this essay, those who served in the Red Cell look back on its history to derive lessons for better navigating this uncertain future. Now is not a time for cautious assessments but fearless exploration. Leaders in the public and private sectors must be ready to navigate a broader range of possible futures. The safety, security, and livelihoods of future generations depend on such forward thinking.

The Origin of the Red Cell

It was September 12, 2001, just 24 hours after the tragic attacks of 9/11. The American people were in shock and struggling to make sense of what had happened. The United States had experienced a strategic surprise as unfathomable as the Pearl Harbor attack in 1941.

At CIA headquarters in Virginia that morning, Director of Central Intelligence George Tenet gathered Deputy Director for Intelligence Jami Miscik and two distinguished analytic managers, Robert Ovelmen and Paul Frandano, to find a way to compel the bureaucracy to go beyond what it knew and what it assessed and to consider what could be. With a simple but bold mandate, “tell me what others don’t” and “make seniors feel uncomfortable,” he commissioned them to create a new analytic unit, called the Red Cell, to challenge conventional wisdom on terrorism. (Foreign Policy) Neither Ovelmen nor Frandano were experts on terrorism or the Middle East, but they were known for their strong analytic skills, exceptional command of history, understanding of policymaker needs, and somewhat quirky personalities. This cell was not limited to traditional Cold War-style “red teaming” that focused on roleplaying the adversary, but instead it was a more expansive effort to explore possibilities.

Tenet gave them great latitude to gather talent from across the intelligence enterprise. While the mission initially was limited to terrorism and the Middle East, the analysts they recruited had worked everything but those issues. Having experienced the unthinkable, these analysts were tasked to stretch their imaginations to consider the full range of plausible next events. The first products were short and pithy, with catchy titles and provocative ideas about the nature of attack and what the coming days and weeks could portend. The first Red Cell analysis was published two days later on 14 September. Tenet took it directly into the Oval Office, and President George W. Bush asked for more.

Within the first year, the Red Cell was tasked to go beyond its original focus on terrorism and branch into other issues. In the run up to the invasion of Iraq in 2003, the Red Cell produced a flurry of products on what Iraqi President Saddam Husayn might do to prevent an attack and how he might react. The presentations and argumentation were deliberately eye-catching and evocative to make readers engage with the ideas and to remember them the next day. Ovelmen and Frandano knew the avalanche of information and meetings senior policymakers faced each day and wanted the ideas to stand out and be considered, even if they were later dismissed.

This strategy was not without controversy. Some ideas were not only bold but contradicted by existing facts. Others unwittingly were uncomfortably close to highly sensitive policies and plans. Some military commanders in the field worried that the Red Cell might give their superiors dangerous ideas. Expert analysts across the IC were often furious, especially if a Red Cell idea created a tasking for them. Sometimes CIA seniors had to remind readers that the Red Cell was not the authoritative assessment. Even with these challenges, the Red Cell continued to have senior-level support. One senior policymaker once said, “tell those analysts I disagree with this but also tell them to keep writing it.” In his 2006 confirmation testimony to become CIA director, General Michael Hayden said, "Red cell alternative analysis and red cell alternative evaluations are a rich source of thought-provoking estimates, and they should be a part, an integral part, of our analysis.” (Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, May 18, 2006)

BOX: Original mission statement: “In response to the events of 11September, the Director of Central Intelligence commissioned CIA ‘s Deputy Director for Intelligence to create a "red cell " that would think unconventionally about the full range of relevant analytic issues. The DCI Red Cell is thus charged with taking a pronounced "out-of-the-box " approach and will periodically produce memoranda and reports intended to provoke thought rather than to provide authoritative assessments.”

The Next Generation – Red Cell 2.0

As the Red Cell approached the end of the decade, the remaining original members planned to retire. They assumed they would be told to turn off the lights and lock the vault. They had a good run! They had many fans and probably an equal number of skeptics. Contrary to their expectations, then–CIA Deputy Director for Analysis Michael Morell tasked them to find a new set of leaders to carry on the work and train the next generation.

However, with greater distance from the tragedy of 9/11, the interest in and tolerance for the most extreme ideas had waned among some audiences. Both policymakers and the intelligence leadership wanted Red Cell products to have more grounding in tradecraft and data while still considering alternative trajectories and expanding thinking on the various possibilities. The new Red Cell leadership recognized the challenge to preserve and maintain the “Redness” while grounding the assessments with rigorous research and data. To meet these competing demands, they launched Red Cell 2.0, refreshing the brand and expanding the style, argumentation, and presentation.

The Red Cell still had top-level support to delve into the thorniest issues. In September 2012, CIA Director David Petraeus reiterated and expanded the mission, telling the Red Cell to “take on our most difficult intelligence challenges” and “shock us.” During this time, both senior military officers and policymakers found value in Red Cell analysis. Lt. General H.R. McMaster recalled that “As National Security Advisor and as a military commander in combat, I found Red Cell papers useful, in part, because they challenged assumptions and were untainted by and often ran counter to policy preferences.”

Other leaders wanted to participate in the brainstormings because Red Cell analysts challenged them. Supreme Allied Commander NATO, Admiral James Stavridis described engaging with the Red Cell team as “an intellectual adventure that forced my senior staff to interrogate our assumptions, consider more extreme futures for the Alliance, and to understand the choices and risks involved in each scenario.” Red Cell engagements often kicked off with a provocative prompt to disarm the participants and to pave the way for a more open and productive conversation. In one such engagement, a Red Cell analyst launched with “sir, if you were indicted for war crimes.” Although taken aback by such an outlandish suggestion, the prompt changed the tenor of the conversation, and this senior leader became a regular consumer of Red Cell analysis.

To add rigor and maintain credibility, the cell directly addressed perceived analytic tradecraft weaknesses, built partnerships with similar units across the US government, systematically interrogated assumptions and biases, and experimented with new ways of conveying analysis. To show their homework, Red Cell analysts sharpened the logic and argumentation of its products and published more point/counterpoint assessments to illuminate both sides of a contentious issue. During this time, CIA leadership reaffirmed the importance of the cell’s mission but encouraged the team to consider scenarios that were smaller deviations from the expected future—rather than being so far out of the box. In response, the Red Cell turned to more multiple scenarios analysis to explore the spectrum of futures from slight variations to more extreme futures. (NPR, May 23, 2012) Some applauded this effort while others complained the Red Cell would lose its edge.

Being a small, experienced, and non-hierarchical unit enabled rapid prototyping. The team experimented with innovative analytic exercises and developed new approaches for delivering complex analytic stories in creative, memorable ways. For example, the team kicked off each year with a highly engaging, day-long exercise called “Ideapalooza” to push beyond the expected future and explore the intersection of trends and dynamics. (Foreign Policy) The Red Cell was the first unit to publish a fully interactive, choose-your-own-adventure, analytic product, enabling analysts and policymakers to test the impact of different variables. The Red Cell experimented with delivering analysis as a graphic novel. To present difficult messages, the Red Cell drew on historical analogies, turns of phrase, and even pop culture. From song references like “Back in the USSR” to puns about the cold when writing about the Arctic to provocative titles like “Anticipating Saddam’s Last Gasp Gambits,” “Saddam’s Eleventh Hour Options,” and “What If the US Is Seen as an Exporter of Terrorism,” the Red Cell pushed the limits to make scenarios vivid and spark the imagination.

While maintaining its creative environment, the Red Cell often tackled some of the most serious and challenging national security questions. The NSC called upon the Red Cell to produce highly speculative, strategic perspectives on global issues that did not lend themselves to more traditional, heavily sourced intelligence products, such as the future of geopolitics, the durability of alliances, and the international order. These products were less challenge analysis and more thought provoking, big picture assessments. The collocation of senior analysts from different disciplines and with experiences working different regions and issues was an advantage in tackling broad, strategic global issues.

Moving from a Cell to a Product Line

In the most significant evolution since the creation of the Red Cell, in 2023 the Red Cell ceased to be a standalone unit and became a product line under the direction of a Red Cell chief. No longer was there a dedicated staff or separate offices. Instead, Red Cells would now be written by the expert analysts, managed and edited by a senior-level analyst in negotiation with regional and issue managers. There are obvious pros and cons to this new approach.

  • On the plus side, products could draw on the expertise of those who know the topic best and can see more nuanced variations. Moreover, when published, the assessments would have high-level support, increasing the possibility of policymakers reading them.
  • However, it is difficult to question your own, well-researched and -reasoned analytic line, especially one that has held up to time and events. During crises, expert analysts rarely have the time to pull away from daily coverage of events to consider alternatives and question assumptions. Human nature is to expect the future to be like the present, and it often requires an outsider who is not burdened by expertise to ask the fundamental questions. For example, in 2011, regional analysts in the early days of the Arab Spring were covering the crisis 24/7 with situation reports and daily assessments. The Red Cell was able to explore provocative questions, such as “is this an end-of-history moment”, and could develop multiple scenarios for how the crisis might end.

Shades of Red

Looking back on this work, Red Cell products have always had many shades of red, ranging from far outside the box—almost crimson analysis—to products that were just a subtle but important deviation from the mainline–pink. Sometimes the situation called for a complete 180-degree contrarian take on how the world could go in the opposite direction, but in other situations the Red Cell looked to stress-test underlying assumptions or pursue multiple scenarios. From the beginning, the Red Cell focused on a few analytic techniques or prompts to help tease out subtleties and other perspectives.

  • A popular and effective approach was What-If analysis. This approach recognized the most likely future trajectory but then asked, what if something changed? These pieces explored both why something different might happen and what the consequences might be.
  • Devil’s Advocacy—a true contrarian alternative—was sometimes but not often the line of argumentation. More frequently, the piece offered a range of ways a situation could evolve or various perspectives a foreign actor might hold.
  • Another favorite but more difficult approach which was used from the beginning was the first-person narrative in which the Red Cell tried to channel the strategies, calculations, and even fears of key leaders like Saddam Husayn and Usama Bin Laden. (CIA Reading Room)
  • An important and analytically rigorous technique was the assumptions check in which the Red Cell would identify and interrogative important underlying assumptions about an issue.
  • Multiple scenarios papers delivered variations of the future from very “red” storylines to trajectories that are largely continuations of the status quo. Some scenarios were mutually exclusive while others offered sequential developments.
  • Team A/B or Point/Counterpoint papers explored opposing explanations or arguments about the future. Sometimes, these were delivered in a debate style.

Assessing the Value of the Red Cell

There are many misconceptions about the role of such a contrarian unit. Many tried to assess the value of Red Cell products based on accuracy, assuming that predicting the future better than the mainline analytic experts was the goal. However, the Red Cell was never designed to be right or to provide authoritative assessments. Judging the value of the Red Cell based on how often its alternative analysis was right misses the point. In fact, the Red Cell should be wrong most of the time, given the exceptional expertise and analysis conducted by the Intelligence Community every day. When the Red Cell was right, the mainline analysis by definition had missed something.

At its core, the mission of the Red Cell was to help US decision-makers prepare for a greater range of possible futures to make our nation safer, stronger, and more resilient in the face of growing uncertainty and to give them decision advantage. The Red Cell achieved this by widening the aperture on any situation and exploring plausible—not necessarily probable—futures. The real value was in making people think, making them curious, provoking debate, and helping them understand the underlying foundations of their assessments. Done right, the Red Cell identified analytic weaknesses and helped make mainline analysis stronger. Helping analytic colleagues strengthen their assessments was more important than delivering a finished product to a senior policymaker.

Here are few ways to consider the value and usefulness:

  • Did decision-makers read it? Yes, some more than others. Many read the analysis even—and especially—if they disagreed with it as a check on their own thinking.
  • Did analysts and warfighters read Red Cells? Absolutely. Red Cell products were among the most read analytic products in the Intelligence Community over multiple years.
  • Did Red Cells spark debate? Almost always. It created discussions, which was the point.
  • Did senior decision-makers ask for Red Cell papers? Quite often.
  • Did Red Cell products influence policy discussions and even choices? Again, yes. In one instance, the NSC reworked a regional strategy in light of a Red Cell memo that foresaw the involvement of a major international player. (Forbes)
  • Did the Red Cell shift and improve the culture of mainline analytic units? Yes. Over time many offices incorporated Red Cell techniques, and some created their own contrarian in-house units. Red Cell alumni often went back to “regular” units, in effect, becoming evangelists for out-of-the-box thinking and analysis.
  • Have others incorporated these techniques and approaches? Yes, in foreign governments, international institutions, and private companies, entities like the Red Cell—some even called the Red Cell—now exist around the world. (Stimson Center) (Red Cell Partners)Georgetown University has created a Master’s Degree that includes Red Cell projects. (Georgetown University) In 2023, the Stimson Center—a Washington-based think tank—created its own unit called the Red Cell which takes “a devil’s advocate approach to US foreign policy” and “puts forward innovative solutions and unorthodox thinking about America’s role in the world.” (Stimson Center)

Secrets of Success

The success of the Red Cell stemmed from the combination of circumstances, design, and leadership. The shock and fear generated by the attacks on 9/11, followed by flawed intelligence assessments of Iraq’s WMD programs, created the environment for more speculative, creative, and provocative analytic assessments. To meet this demand, CIA leadership made several important choices to create a unique unit with the authority to explore, question, challenge, and go beyond the data. Moreover, they let the ideas be heard, even when they were on the edge and even when they disagreed with them. However, over time, as memories of 9/11 faded, the conditions that facilitated and protected bold analysis evaporated or were dismantled one after another.

Top Cover: With a mandate to make leaders uncomfortable, success required absolute assurance and top cover. That top cover came from both senior analytic managers and senior customers and was reiterated often in the early days.

The Process: The Red Cell also was given the freedom to write and publish without going through formal Intelligence Community coordination processes. The Red Cell was required to consult, but not to coordinate. It could—and often did—disagree with the mainline, coordinated point of view. It weighed the evidence differently. It took speculative leaps. In contrast, mainline analysis had to reflect the views and expertise of the entire organization; every analytic unit with a stake in the topic got to weigh in, and the originating office was obligated to take these views on board. Judgments had to be rigorously supported with multiple citations and sources. This process is what made the end result an CIA product, not an individual one. It ensured that all the evidence is considered and all defensible points of view are reflected. A great deal of time and effort went into coordination, and it was a point of pride for analysts to do it well and come up with an agreed analytic line.

Talent and Staffing: Being a member of and writing for the Red Cell required insatiable curiosity, a willingness to ask tough questions and go against the grain, and a propensity to see angles others didn’t. Red Cell analysts had to be fearless and willing to speak truth to power no matter the consequences. To find such talent, CIA leaders gave the Red Cell authority to recruit from across the organization and request officers from other agencies, including those senior analysts who had topped out and thus, had little fear of pushing analytic boundaries. The cell combined a few core, long-term members with frequent rotations, including from other agencies, to bring fresh ideas and new energy.

Location: Having a designated team outside of the organizational chart and physically separate from expert teams was a key component of the cell’s success. Experts can be too close to a topic or an analytic line to question it. The Red Cell could step back and see a broader landscape of possibilities.

Culture: The Red Cell was about ideas above all else and promoted a culture of exploration, play, and divergent thinking. Rank was left at the door–even for senior military officers. The work always started with conversation/brainstorming—not an unusual method—but in the cell brainstorming sessions preceded every analytic effort. The art of the conversation is teasing out ideas first. Collaboration was another critical component; Red Cell analysts often co-authored products or developed projects with other offices, agencies, governments, academia, and the private sector. No one has a monopoly on innovation or good ideas.

Conveying Analysis: Creativity in argumentation and presentation brought the unlikely future scenarios to life for skeptical consumers. The Red Cell experimented with new formats, visual aids, and graphics, and it worked closely with designers, cartographers and videographers.

Lessons for an Uncertain Future

Twenty-five years since the establishment of the Red Cell, the future environment appears even more uncertain, more prone to unprecedented disruptions, and potentially more dangerous. The combination of rapidly advancing technologies, hyper connectivity, changing international norms and institutions, discontented publics, and the return of great-power competition has created a world in flux. Change is happening at a breathtaking pace and scale with implications for our security, stability, and prosperity. Dynamics that were unimaginable even five years ago are now reality.

Experience continues to show the high probability of being surprised by low-probability events. Organizations of all types remain vulnerable to groupthink, confirmation bias, and assuming the future will be like the present. Such well-known organizational and human behaviors lie at the root of historical policy and intelligence failures. Red Cell-type organizations help guard against these tendencies and compel consideration of alternatives.

To anticipate, manage, and thrive in these divergent futures, now is the time for more Red Cell-like thinking in every sector—both public and private. Leaders and decision-makers must be ready to navigate a broader range of possible futures, including inevitable strategic surprises. Now is not a time for cautious assessments but fearless exploration. The safety, security, and livelihoods of future generations depend on such forward thinking.

Drawing on our years of analytic experience and thinking the unthinkable, this group of Red Cell alumni offers several suggestions to improve future readiness for our communities, our industries, and our country.

  • Institutionalize a challenge function: Create a dedicated effort with a broad mandate and direct, unfettered access to the top leadership (CEOs, directors, commanders, etc.) Such a team should be charged with challenging assumptions, questioning longstanding practices, and exploring low probability-high impact scenarios.
  • Explore a broader range of futures: Stress-test goals and policies across a range of plausible futures to improve resilience, increase flexibility, and take advantage of emerging opportunities.
  • Think multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary: Dynamics and trends can no longer be analyzed in isolation. The world is too complex and connected.
  • Go beyond the obvious: It is in the second- and third-order implications where surprises tend to occur, often from seemingly small development that cascade over time.
  • Give permission to fail: Instill a ”start-up” mindset, where many investments are dead-ends but a few pay off in a big way.
  • Be FEARLESS. The world is depending on you.

item.title: Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying
item.description:
Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying Expert comment jon.wallace 24 September 2026

Denmark used its soft power to rally support and took the dispute out of the limelight – addressing underlying US interests instead of President Trump’s unacceptable public position.

This week, Denmark has extricated itself from a period of coercive US diplomacy over Greenland. The agreement announced on 22 September elegantly resolves the dispute over the territory, without forcing Denmark or the government of Greenland to give up very much. 

Even before the dispute, Denmark had indicated it would be content to increase the number of US bases in Greenland and enhance US access to them. These measures were already possible under an existing 1951 agreement. 

The new agreement adds an undertaking by Denmark and Greenland to refuse major investments from non-members of the EU or NATO that would grant them a foothold in strategic Arctic areas. Again, on this point, Washington was pushing on an open door.

The only meaningful change concerns the mechanism to ensure that this arrangement will be permanent. The 1951 agreement, amended in 2004, also does not expire. But the new text adds that Greenland will remain part of NATO and continue to comply with the agreement, should it opt for independence. 

An independent Greenland might have been willing to retain the US bases and related agreements anyway. After all, it would need to rely on US defence support and a NATO security guarantee. But expressly making these points in an agreement co-signed by Greenland overcame the deal-breaker of President Donald Trump’s demand for sovereignty over all of Greenland or at least the US base areas.

The agreement represents a masterclass by Denmark in using the classical art of diplomacy to overcome bullying, in an age of changing geopolitics and unstable global governance. 

Indeed, the steps Denmark took to resolve the dispute provide valuable insight into how countries can defend their interests in the face of apparently overwhelming pressure.

Step 1: Isolate the bully and call the game

In January this year, President Trump declared that the US would need to ‘own’ Greenland to prevent Russia or China from taking it, and to ensure US national security. He even raised the option of a military takeover of the territory.

The president may have believed opposition would be minimal. Just days before, EU and NATO countries had been unwilling to confront him publicly over the armed US intervention against Venezuela, despite it being a clear breach of international law. In the emergency meeting of the UN Security Council that followed, they had stayed meekly silent. 

Greenland was different. Denmark could clearly assert that Trump was placing the future of NATO in peril. Hence, Denmark could show that the US action posed a threat to both the territorial integrity of Denmark and to the security of all states in Western Europe. Accordingly, NATO countries and EU members overcame their hesitancy to upset the White House, and strongly and unanimously rejected his demand. Indeed, they went further, dispatching a European defence mission to Greenland, supposedly as a matter of routine.

Calling out the US’s game for what it was – a demand to surrender national territory under the threat of force at a time when the West was resisting Putin’s assault on Ukraine – was crucial in rallying support.

Step 2: Enter the fray with clean hands

In this dispute, Denmark continually had the advantage in the battle for international sympathy. It entered the fray with clean hands, taking advantage of its soft power, which has been nurtured over decades of sensitive advocacy for justice in relation to the Global South and the international rule of law. The US under Trump, on the other hand, has caused continued upset throughout, as a result of its military actions and other activity such as the president’s sweeping ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs.

The US could also not accuse Denmark of hypocrisy over any supposed colonial legacy relating to Greenland. By 1954, the UN General Assembly had determined that Greenland had freely decided to integrate with Denmark on the basis of equal constitutional and administrative standing with other parts of Denmark. 

By 1979 Copenhagen offered home rule. Two decades later, in 2009, it granted wide-ranging self-government to Greenland. Crucially, this 2009 arrangement included an express right of self-determination for the people of Greenland, with a provision to opt for independence. Any sale of Greenland (as Trump had previously proposed) or its transfer to the US against the wishes of the population, would have violated this existing right to self-determination. 

This meant that throughout the dispute, Denmark could claim a role as both the upholder of the international right to self-determination, and the defender of its own territorial integrity.

Step 3: Clarify the legal status

President Trump sought to enhance his claim by suggesting that Denmark did not have a clear title to Greenland. In view of the 2009 agreement’s self-determination provisions, this assertion became less relevant. In any event, it was easy to prove that Denmark held good title. And the US clearly had none at all. 

In 1916 US Secretary of State Robert Lansing issued a declaration accepting Denmark’s claim to the island. When the US took over the defence of Greenland during Germany’s occupation of Denmark during the Second World War, it did so in ‘recognition and respect for the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Denmark over Greenland.’ 

This expressly included Danish sovereignty over base areas constructed by the US. The post-war agreements on defence cooperation and US bases of 1951 and 2004 also consistently confirmed Danish sovereignty. Indeed, in an amazing reversal of the US position, so does the new 2026 agreement. The text reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and acknowledges Greenland’s right to self-determination. 

Step 4: Dial the temperature down and let experts do the work

When encountering the US, Denmark was careful to avoid a public confrontation with Trump in front of cameras, learning from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s experience at the Oval Office in 2025. 

Instead, when the row intensified, Copenhagen dispatched Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen to Washington. As foreign minister, protocol demanded that he should meet with the slightly more moderate US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, instead of the president. 

Vice President JD Vance almost derailed this cunning plan when he insisted on leading the meeting and moving it to the White House. But Rasmussen, a former Danish prime minister, calmly focused on shared security interests in the Arctic. And he remained steadfast where sovereignty and the rights of Greenlanders were concerned.

After a supposed breakthrough on the issue at the Davos conference later in January 2026, Denmark managed to divert dialogue to technical meetings, held confidentially, outside of the public eye. This was the critical change that allowed Copenhagen to defang the entire episode.

Step 5: Focus on interests, not positions

Negotiations experts know that success depends on persuading the sides to step away from their incompatible, publicly stated position and instead address their underlying interests. In this instance, President Trump had claimed that only full sovereignty over Greenland would answer US security needs. 

At Davos, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte offered the US sovereignty at least over its base areas in Greenland. Trump seized that initiative and accepted, withdrawing his threat of invasion. 

However, neither Denmark nor Greenland representatives had been party to that proposal. Handing over even a part of sovereign territory would hardly be acceptable to their parliaments.

But in the technical discussions, it became possible to move from a flat-out demand for sovereignty, to achieving the underlying US desire: a permanent arrangement safeguarding its interests in Greenland. 

Step 6: Be generous in victory

On signing the agreement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was careful to avoid any sense of climb-down by President Trump. It is a deal that can ‘last forever,’ she said, reflecting Trump’s claim that he had achieved an outcome just as permanent as a transfer of sovereignty.

As President Trump’s original stated position was that ‘the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity’, this new agreement seems a clear victory for calm and quiet Danish diplomacy. And it plainly illustrates the power of unity among NATO states and EU members. The lessons for future dealings with great powers are clear.
